title: Uthman's caliphate
hook: the gentle Uthman rules as lands and a navy grow

segments.voice: Yesterday: Umar's death. Struck at the dawn prayer, he left the choice to a council of six. Your line was a council, not a crown.

Should I not feel shy before a man the angels feel shy before? Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, asking that about one of his companions. The scene is small. The Prophet is resting at home, his clothes loosely arranged. Abu Bakr comes in, and he stays as he is. Umar comes in, and he stays as he is. Then Uthman asks to enter, and the Prophet sits up and straightens his garment. Aisha asks him why. His answer is that question. After Umar's death, the council chose this man: Uthman ibn Affan.
screen: `THE PROPHET SITS UP.` → `THE ANGELS FEEL SHY.` → `THE COUNCIL CHOOSES UTHMAN.`

segments.voice: Bukhari records how. The men Umar named narrowed it among themselves, and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, giving up his own claim, was trusted to choose between Ali and Uthman. He spent nights consulting people, the report says, then took Uthman's hand and pledged to him, and the people followed. Uthman came with a reputation. In Bukhari's reports he answered the Prophet's call to provide the well of Rumah for the people, and to equip the army in a time of hardship. Wealthy, quiet, generous, modest. Under his rule the lands of the Muslims kept growing, and something new happened: ships. Bukhari tells of Umm Haram, who heard the Prophet describe people of his community riding the sea like kings on thrones, and asked him to pray she would be one of them. The report says she later sailed, in the days of Mu'awiyah, Uthman's governor of Syria, and the histories set that voyage in Uthman's time. Now the harder part. Gentleness in a ruler reads two ways. His admirers see mercy: a caliph slow to punish, open-handed with his own money. His critics, in his own lifetime, said he gave too many posts to relatives and was too slow to remove governors people complained about. The sources record both. Sunni Muslims honor him as the third rightly guided caliph and one of the companions promised paradise. Shia Muslims hold that Ali should have led from the start, and Shia tellings dwell on the complaints. Both readings sit side by side here, because the complaints will grow.
screen: `ABD AL-RAHMAN CONSULTS FOR NIGHTS.` · `A WELL PROVIDED, AN ARMY EQUIPPED.` · `UMM HARAM AND THE SEA.` · `MERCY, OR TOO SOFT?` · then, large: `GENTLE RULE.`

segments.voice: Pick one small kingdom where others depend on your decisions: a kitchen, a classroom, a shift you run, even a dog. Remember a moment there when you were sharper than you needed to be, and replay it with the same firmness and a softer voice. If you pray, you can ask for mercy in how you lead.
Uthman's caliphate: a modest, generous man chosen by the council after Umar, a time of growth and ships at sea, and complaints that would not go away. Today's word.
Your line: gentle rule. Firm and gentle can live in the same voice. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sunni Muslims honor Uthman as the third rightly guided caliph and remember his modesty and generosity; Shia Muslims hold that Ali was the rightful leader, and Shia tellings dwell on the complaints against Uthman's rule.

original.note: Arabic: the name of the third caliph for Sunni Muslims, Uthman ibn Affan.

trapdoor: what you thought: Uthman was just the caliph between Umar and Ali.

what a scholar hears: Bukhari's account of the council and Umm Haram's sea voyage under Mu'awiyah, and the long Sunni and Shia debate over Uthman's appointments.

notes: Audit: 'the report places the sea voyage in this era' overstated Bukhari (which says only 'in the days of Mu'awiyah'); dating it to Uthman's caliphate is now attributed to the histories (al-Tabari). 'Hold both views without picking a winner' (an instruction to the listener) recast as a description. Note: the earlier note about 'many of their historians are critical' is stale; that wording is no longer in the script.
The hook opens with a paraphrase (no quotation marks) of the Prophet's question in Sahih Muslim 2401; confirm wording.

Hadith numbers cited from memory: confirm Muslim 2401, Bukhari 3700, 2778 (ta'liq on Rumah and the army of hardship), and the Umm Haram reports (2788–2789, 2799–2800). Confirm that the report places her voyage 'in the days of Mu'awiyah'.
The outline's 'rules twelve years' was cut under the claims rule. 'The first ships' was also avoided; the script says only 'ships at sea'.
Sunni and Shia views are given side by side; 'many of their historians are critical' should be confirmed as fair by both Keepers.
The council members are not counted on purpose; yesterday (876) covered the council of six.
